q: How much electricity and CO2 does a -80 C lab freezer use, and does raising it to -70 C help?
title: ULT freezer energy and CO2
short: Measure it: plug a meter on the freezer for a week, multiply kWh per day by 365 and by 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh. Raising the setpoint from -80 C to -70 C usually cuts use, but by an amount that depends on the model, so measure before and after rather than trusting a headline percentage.
audience: Pharma R&D, CRO, biobank and hospital lab managers

sections.h: Getting a kWh figure you can defend
ol: Best: a plug-in energy meter or a sub-meter on the freezer's circuit for at least seven days of normal use, including door openings.
Next best: the rated kWh per day on the model's datasheet or energy label, recorded as rated, not measured.
Avoid nameplate power in watts x 24 hours. The compressor cycles, so that overstates use.

p: Record a week at -80 C, change the setpoint, let it settle for a day, then record a week at -70 C with similar door use. The difference in kWh per day is your saving for that unit. Before changing anything, get sign-off from the sample owner or QA. Validated storage conditions for regulated or GMP samples must not change on an energy argument alone.

sections.h: Costs that do not show on the freezer meter
ul: Heat: every kWh the freezer draws ends up as heat in the room, which the AC then has to remove. Freezer rooms often need more cooling than the freezers suggest.
Refrigerant: check the gas on the nameplate. A leak or a recharge is Scope 1 in kg CO2e at that gas's GWP; some newer units use hydrocarbon refrigerants with very low GWP.
Age and upkeep: iced-up door seals and dusty condenser filters raise use. Defrosting and cleaning are cheap first steps.

p: Freezer kWh are already inside your electricity bill, so do not add them on top of Scope 2. Use the freezer figure to see what share of the bill the freezers take and to rank savings, such as consolidating half-empty units.

example.title: Worked example: one -80 C freezer
lines: Measured at -80 C: 11.0 kWh per day; at -70 C: 9.2 kWh per day (example readings)
Saving: (11.0 minus 9.2) x 365 = 657 kWh a year
CO2 saved: 657 x 0.710 = 466 kg CO2 a year, before any AC saving
example.note: Readings are illustrative. Use your own meter data.
